title: Auto Mechanics
summary: Learn how vehicles work and how to maintain them: the four-stroke engine, lubrication, cooling and fuel systems, vehicle electrics and diagnostics, transmission, brakes, steering and tyres, servicing and fuel economy, and hybrids, EVs and careers. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Apprentices, drivers, fleet staff and anyone starting in motor mechanics

body.p: Most vehicles still use internal combustion engines that burn petrol or diesel inside cylinders. Pistons move up and down, turning a crankshaft through connecting rods, which drives the wheels through the transmission.

steps: Intake: the piston moves down and draws in air (and fuel in many petrol engines) through the open inlet valve.
Compression: both valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the mixture.
Power: the mixture burns (lit by a spark plug in petrol engines, or by the heat of compression in diesels), forcing the piston down.
Exhaust: the piston moves up and pushes burnt gases out through the exhaust valve.

body.p: Displacement is the swept volume of all cylinders. A four-cylinder engine with an 86 mm bore and 86 mm stroke displaces π/4 x 8.6² x 8.6 x 4, about 1998 cm³, sold as a 2.0-litre engine. Compression ratio compares the volume with the piston at the bottom to the volume at the top: with 500 cm³ swept and 55 cm³ clearance per cylinder, it is (500 + 55) / 55, about 10.1 : 1. Diesels use much higher ratios.

body.tip: Knocking, loss of power or blue or black exhaust smoke are early signs of engine problems; investigate them promptly.

list: Lubrication: oil reduces friction and wear, carries away heat and keeps parts clean. Check the oil level with the dipstick on level ground with the engine off, and change oil and filter at the intervals in the service book.

Cooling: a water pump circulates coolant through the engine and radiator; a thermostat controls temperature, and a fan helps at low speed. Overheating can warp the cylinder head. Never open a hot radiator cap.
Fuel system: a pump sends fuel from the tank through a filter to injectors, controlled by the engine computer. Dirty fuel and clogged filters are common problems on African roads.
Air intake: a clean air filter is vital in dusty conditions; a blocked one cuts power and raises fuel use.
Ignition (petrol): coils and spark plugs provide the spark at the right moment.
Exhaust: carries gases away; the catalytic converter reduces harmful emissions.

body.p: Belts (timing belt or chain, and auxiliary belts) keep these systems synchronised and driven. A broken timing belt can wreck an engine, so replace it at the recommended interval.

body.tip: Most engine failures start with neglected oil, coolant or air filters; these cheap checks prevent expensive repairs.

body.p: Vehicles use a 12 V electrical system (24 V in many trucks and buses). The battery starts the engine and powers electrics when the engine is off; the alternator charges the battery and supplies power while running.

list: A fully charged 12 V battery reads about 12.6 V at rest; around 12.0 V means it is largely discharged.
With the engine running, charging voltage is typically about 13.8 to 14.4 V; lower suggests an alternator or belt problem.
The starter motor draws a very large current for a few seconds.
Fuses protect circuits; always replace a fuse with one of the same rating, and find the cause if it blows again.
Modern vehicles use many sensors and electronic control units (ECUs) connected by a network (CAN bus).

body.p: When a warning light appears, an OBD-II scan tool plugged into the diagnostic port reads fault codes, such as codes for a misfire or a faulty oxygen sensor. The code points to a system to test; it does not always identify the faulty part, so confirm with measurements before replacing parts.

body.tip: A digital multimeter and an OBD-II scanner are the two most valuable diagnostic tools for a modern mechanic.

body.p: The clutch (in manual cars) connects and disconnects the engine from the gearbox. The gearbox provides different ratios: low gears for starting and climbing, high gears for cruising. Automatics use a torque converter or clutches to change gear themselves. The final drive and differential let the wheels turn at different speeds around corners.

list: Pressing the pedal pushes brake fluid through pipes to calipers or wheel cylinders (hydraulics), forcing pads against discs or shoes against drums.
Worn pads squeal or grind; replace them before metal touches the disc.
Brake fluid absorbs water over time and should be changed as the service book says.
A soft or spongy pedal means air or a leak in the system: do not drive until it is fixed.
ABS prevents wheels locking during hard braking.

body.p: Shock absorbers and springs keep tyres in contact with the road. Wheel alignment affects tyre wear and handling. A tyre size of 195/65 R15 means 195 mm wide, a sidewall 65% of the width (about 126.75 mm), on a 15-inch rim, giving an overall diameter of about 381 + 253.5 = 634.5 mm.

body.tip: Check tyre pressures monthly when the tyres are cold, using the figures on the door pillar or manual.

list: Change engine oil and oil filter.
Check and replace air and fuel filters as needed.
Inspect belts, hoses, coolant and brake fluid levels.
Check brakes, tyres, lights, wipers and battery terminals.
Look underneath for leaks and damaged parts.
Record the service and mileage.

body.p: Fuel consumption is often given in litres per 100 km. A car using 40 litres over 500 km uses 40 / 500 x 100 = 8 L/100 km. A 300 km trip then needs about 24 litres; at R23.50 a litre, that is about R564. Under-inflated tyres, blocked air filters, aggressive driving and carrying excess weight all increase consumption.

Never work under a vehicle supported only by a jack: use axle stands on firm ground and chock the wheels. Disconnect the battery before electrical work, beware of hot exhausts and coolant, and handle used oil properly; it pollutes water and soil.

body.tip: Keep a simple logbook in the car; well-documented maintenance raises resale value.

body.p: Vehicles are changing quickly. Hybrid vehicles combine an engine with an electric motor and battery, and electric vehicles (EVs) run entirely on batteries, with far fewer moving parts. Electric motorcycles and minibuses are growing in cities such as Nairobi and Kigali, and many are assembled locally.

list: EVs and hybrids use high-voltage systems, often hundreds of volts, shown by orange cables. Only trained technicians with insulated tools and the right procedures should work on them.
Servicing shifts towards batteries, power electronics, software and brakes, tyres and suspension.
Diagnostics increasingly rely on computers and manufacturer software.

body.p: Motor mechanics train through apprenticeships, technical colleges and trade tests. Specialisations include diesel and heavy vehicles, auto electrics, panel beating and spray painting, motorcycles, agricultural machinery and EVs. Many mechanics run their own workshops; honesty, clear quotes and explaining repairs to customers build loyalty.

body.tip: Learn auto electrics and diagnostics; they are where many mechanics are short of skills and where earnings are higher.
